output.query: cardiac sarcoidosis AV block diagnosis device immunosuppression guideline

results.summary: Cardiac sarcoidosis is diagnosed on myocardial histology, or clinically when extracardiac sarcoidosis is proven histologically together with at least one cardiac feature (for example Mobitz II or third-degree AV block, unexplained sustained VT, LVEF below 40%, patchy uptake on dedicated cardiac FDG-PET or late enhancement on CMR in a compatible pattern) and other causes are reasonably excluded. Patients younger than 60 with unexplained Mobitz II or third-degree AV block should be evaluated for cardiac sarcoidosis (Class IIa). In patients with an indication for pacing an ICD can be useful (Class IIa), and device implantation can be useful even if the AV block reverses. Immunosuppression can be useful in Mobitz II or third-degree AV block.
results.title: HRS expert consensus statement on the diagnosis and management of arrhythmias associated with cardiac sarcoidosis (Birnie DH et al., Heart Rhythm 2014;11:1305-1323)

results.summary: Permanent pacing is indicated (Class I) for third-degree or high-degree AV block irrespective of symptoms when no reversible cause is present. In patients younger than 60 with new unexplained AV block, cardiac imaging (CMR, or FDG-PET when sarcoidosis is suspected) should be considered to look for a specific cause. In cardiac sarcoidosis with an indication for permanent pacing, an ICD should be considered.

general.query: syncope initial evaluation and risk stratification

results.key_finding: Initial evaluation comprises history, physical examination including supine and standing blood pressure, and a 12-lead ECG. High-risk features (syncope during exertion or supine, palpitations before the event, known structural or coronary disease, family history of sudden death under 40, high-risk ECG findings) call for early in-hospital evaluation with immediate ECG monitoring. Echocardiography is indicated when structural heart disease is known or suspected; EEG, brain imaging and routine laboratory panels are not recommended without a specific indication.
results.title: 2018 ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of syncope (Brignole M et al., Eur Heart J 2018;39:1883-1948)

results.key_finding: Risk stratification at the initial evaluation separates patients needing in-hospital monitoring and cardiac testing from those suitable for outpatient evaluation; targeted rather than routine blood testing is advised.
results.title: 2017 ACC/AHA/HRS Guideline for the evaluation and management of patients with syncope (Shen WK et al.)

general.summary: Guidelines base syncope work-up on the initial evaluation (history, examination, orthostatic BP, 12-lead ECG) and risk stratification; high-risk patients receive in-hospital ECG monitoring and targeted cardiac testing.

clinical_pearls: Cardiac sarcoidosis is a leading specific cause of high-grade AV block in adults under 60 and should be sought in unexplained complete AV block in this age group
Serum ACE is often normal in sarcoidosis, particularly with cardiac involvement, and cannot exclude it
Uveitis, hilar lymphadenopathy, arthralgia and cough point to systemic sarcoidosis; isolated cardiac involvement also occurs
Cardiac FDG-PET needs dietary suppression of physiological myocardial glucose uptake; patchy septal uptake with FDG-avid hilar nodes is the classic pattern
Sarcoid granulomas produce 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D independently of PTH, so vitamin D supplementation can provoke hypercalcaemia
metadata.condition_name: Cardiac syncope (Cardiac Sarcoidosis with Complete AV Block)
metadata.diagnostic_trap: Normal serum ACE in cardiac sarcoidosis; untreated subclinical hypothyroidism (TSH 6.4, normal free T4) as an alternative explanation for bradycardia; a prior anxiety label deflecting the work-up from cardiac disease; convulsive syncope mistaken for a seizure
metadata.difficulty_rationale: Six required steps (ECG, targeted labs, TTE, telemetry, cardiac FDG-PET, EBUS-TBNA) with chest imaging, cardiac MRI and the drug review recommended; three red herrings (normal ACE, raised TSH, anxiety label); the ECG is diagnostic of complete AV block, but its cause in a 42-year-old needs cardiac imaging and extracardiac histology, and the normal ACE invites a false exclusion.

patient.history_present_illness:
Ms. Eleanor Hartley is a 42-year-old Caucasian woman, a middle school science teacher, who presents to the emergency department via EMS after her husband called 911 when he found her unresponsive on the kitchen floor. According to her husband, she had been eating breakfast and stood up from the table when she suddenly lost consciousness and fell sideways to the floor. She did not call out or appear to have any warning. He observed brief rhythmic movements of her arms and legs lasting approximately 8-10 seconds before she became still. She did not appear cyanotic during the event. She was unresponsive for approximately 25-30 seconds in total, then became aware, looked confused for 10-15 seconds, then asked 'did I fall?' She was immediately oriented and conversational and denied any focal neurological symptoms. EMS arrived 6 minutes later and documented a slow regular rhythm at 36-38 bpm on the cardiac monitor. Blood glucose on scene was 94 mg/dL. EMS administered 1 mg atropine IV with a transient increase in heart rate to 58 bpm that was not sustained. She was transported to the ED with a pacing-ready external defibrillator in place.

The patient herself reports that over the past two months she has experienced three episodes of lightheadedness and presyncope with position change from sitting to standing, each resolving within 30-60 seconds. She did not seek care, attributing these to her anxiety and possible dehydration. She also endorses progressive fatigue, mild exertional dyspnea (worse over the past 6 weeks), and a dry cough that she assumed was related to her asthma. She denies chest pain, sustained palpitations, orthopnea, or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea.

Of note, she was evaluated by her optometrist approximately 6 weeks ago for bilateral blurry vision and photophobia and was told she had bilateral anterior uveitis of unknown cause; an ophthalmology referral was placed but the appointment had not yet occurred.

Her husband endorses that she has seemed 'unusually tired' for the past 2 months and reports she has had intermittent arthralgias in her hands and knees without swelling. She has a maternal aunt with diagnosed pulmonary sarcoidosis.

Her anxiety disorder history had been previously discussed with her primary care physician as a potential cause of her palpitations and fatigue, and she was reassured that her symptoms were likely anxiety-related at a visit 5 weeks ago. She was not started on any new medications at that visit.

neurological_exam.additional: No tongue laceration. No oral trauma. Small bruise on right hip from the fall. Cardiac exam: bradycardic rate approximately 38 bpm, rhythm regular. No murmurs, rubs, or gallops. Mild bilateral non-tender cervical lymphadenopathy with 1 cm nodes palpable at bilateral posterior cervical chains and submandibular region. Mild bilateral pretibial edema (1+). No skin rash. Conjunctival injection bilaterally.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose testing accurate bilaterally. Heel-to-shin smooth. Rapid alternating movements intact.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: CN II: Visual acuity 20/30 bilaterally; mild bilateral ciliary flush on penlight inspection; slit-lamp examination not available in the emergency department. Pupils equal, round, reactive 4mm to 2mm bilaterally, no afferent pupillary defect. Visual fields full to confrontation. Fundoscopy (undilated): optic discs sharp bilaterally, no papilledema; view slightly hazy. CN III/IV/VI: Extraocular movements intact, no nystagmus, no diplopia. CN V: Sensation intact in V1-V3 bilaterally, masseter symmetric. CN VII: Face symmetric at rest and with activation, no facial weakness. CN VIII: Hearing grossly intact. CN IX/X: Palate elevates symmetrically, gag intact. CN XI: SCM and trapezius 5/5. CN XII: Tongue midline, no atrophy or fasciculations.
neurological_exam.gait: Normal stride, base, and arm swing. Tandem gait intact. Romberg negative.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert, oriented to person, place, and time. GCS 15. Speech fluent and coherent, normal rate and prosody. No confusion, no post-ictal features. Mood anxious but fully cooperative. Attention intact. Recalls 3/3 objects at 5 minutes. No disorientation.
neurological_exam.motor: Bulk and tone normal throughout. Strength 5/5 in all major muscle groups bilaterally. No pronator drift. No fasciculations.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Biceps 2+ bilaterally, triceps 2+ bilaterally, brachioradialis 2+ bilaterally, patellar 2+ bilaterally, Achilles 2+ bilaterally. Plantar responses flexor (downgoing) bilaterally. No clonus.
neurological_exam.sensory: Light touch, pinprick, proprioception, and vibration intact and symmetric throughout all four extremities. No sensory level.
